claim: The Drosophila genome harbors only one voltage-gated sodium channel called Paralytic (Para).
source: The Drosophila genome harbors only one voltage-gated sodium channel called Paralytic (Para), which is required for the generation of all action potentials (Kroll et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kroll et al., 2015.

claim: Para is required for the generation of all action potentials in Drosophila.
source: The Drosophila genome harbors only one voltage-gated sodium channel called Paralytic (Para), which is required for the generation of all action potentials (Kroll et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kroll et al., 2015.

claim: The endogenous para locus was tagged with mCherry in paramCherry flies.
source: To study the localization of Para and to test whether Drosophila glia affects its localization, we and others tagged the endogenous para locus with all predicted isoforms being modified (Ravenscroft et al., 2020; Venken et al., 2011; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ravenscroft et al., 2020 and Venken et al., 2011, and by Figure 1A showing the tagging strategy.

claim: In paramCherry flies, monomeric Cherry (mCherry) is inserted close to the Para N-terminus.
source: In paramCherry flies, monomeric Cherry (mCherry) is inserted close to the Para N-terminus (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 1A showing the insertion site.

claim: Homozygous or hemizygous paramCherry flies are viable with only mildly affected channel function.
source: Homozygous or hemizygous paramCherry flies are viable with only mildly affected channel function (Figure 1B; Ravenscroft et al., 2020; Venken et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 1B showing recovery time data and citations to Ravenscroft et al., 2020 and Venken et al., 2011.

claim: ParamCherry localizes along many CNS and PNS axons of the larval nervous system.
source: ParamCherry localizes along many CNS and PNS axons of the larval nervous system (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C; Ravenscroft et al., 2020; Venken et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C and citations to Ravenscroft et al., 2020 and Venken et al., 2011.

claim: Anti-Para antibodies detect a protein of >250 kDa in size in western blots.
source: In western blots, anti-Para antibodies detect a band of the expected size (>250 kDa), which is shifted toward a higher molecular weight in protein extracts of homozygous paramCherry animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1D showing western blot data.

claim: The Para protein band is shifted toward a higher molecular weight in protein extracts of homozygous paramCherry animals.
source: In western blots, anti-Para antibodies detect a band of the expected size (>250 kDa), which is shifted toward a higher molecular weight in protein extracts of homozygous paramCherry animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1D showing western blot data.

claim: Anti-Para antibodies detect Para localization in control first instar larvae but not in age-matched para null mutant animals.
source: Immunohistochemistry detects Para localization in control first instar larvae but not in age-matched para null mutant animals, further validating the specificity of the antibodies (Figure 1D–E').
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 1D–E' showing immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Endogenously mCherry-tagged Para protein reflects the wild typic Para localization.
source: Thus, we anticipate that endogenously mCherry-tagged Para protein reflects the wild typic Para localization.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the validation experiments showing that the tagged protein behaves similarly to the endogenous protein.

claim: Para appears to evenly localize along the abdominal nerves in cholinergic sensory neurons of third instar larvae.
source: Knockdown of mCherry expression in glutamatergic motor neurons (Mahr and Aberle, 2006) reveals paramCherry expression in cholinergic sensory neurons of third instar larvae. Here, Para appears to evenly localize along the abdominal nerves and is found at many processes within the CNS (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2A showing Para localization in sensory neurons and a citation to Mahr and Aberle, 2006.

claim: Para localizes predominantly in an axonal segment of motor axons at the PNS/CNS boundary of third instar larvae.
source: In contrast, silencing paramCherry in cholinergic neurons (Salvaterra and Kitamoto, 2001) reveals a predominant localization of Para in an axonal segment of motor axons at the PNS/CNS boundary of third instar larvae (Figure 2B), as suggested before (Ravenscroft et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2B showing Para localization in motor neurons and citations to Salvaterra and Kitamoto, 2001 and Ravenscroft et al., 2020.

claim: The Shaker potassium channel is found mostly in the synaptic neuropil regions.
source: Using endogenously tagged proteins, we find the Shaker potassium channel mostly in the synaptic neuropil regions (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2C showing Shaker localization.

claim: The distribution of Shab resembles ParamCherry localization in sensory axons.
source: The distribution of Shab resembles ParamCherry localization in sensory axons (Figure 2A and D), whereas Shal localizes in a pattern similar to Para localization on motor axons (Figure 2B and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 2A and 2D showing Shab and Para localization patterns.

claim: Shal localizes in a pattern similar to Para localization on motor axons.
source: The distribution of Shab resembles ParamCherry localization in sensory axons (Figure 2A and D), whereas Shal localizes in a pattern similar to Para localization on motor axons (Figure 2B and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 2B and 2E showing Shal and Para localization patterns.

claim: Drosophila larval motor axons have an axonal segment resembling the vertebrate AIS harboring both voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels.
source: Thus, Drosophila larval motor axons appear to have an axonal segment resembling the vertebrate AIS harboring both voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the co-localization of Para and Shal channels in motor axons.

claim: Global Para localization in the adult CNS detected by anti-Para antibodies matches the ParamCherry signal.
source: Here, too, global Para localization, as detected by anti-Para antibodies, matched the ParamCherry signal (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 2F and 2G showing Para localization in adult CNS.

claim: Flp expression in all motor neurons results in strong labeling of Para localization at a small part of the axon as it leaves the neuropil in adult flies.
source: In paraFlpTag flies (Fendl et al., 2020), Flp expression in all motor neurons results in strong labeling of Para localization at a small part of the axon as it leaves the neuropil (Figure 2H and H', arrowheads), indicating that an AIS is also found in adult motor axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 2H and H' showing Para localization in adult motor neurons and a citation to Fendl et al., 2020.

claim: An AIS is found in adult motor axons.
source: In paraFlpTag flies (Fendl et al., 2020), Flp expression in all motor neurons results in strong labeling of Para localization at a small part of the axon as it leaves the neuropil (Figure 2H and H', arrowheads), indicating that an AIS is also found in adult motor axons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the localized Para expression pattern and is supported by Figure 2H and H'.

claim: Expression of Flp in all sensory neurons reveals an even Para decoration of axons as they enter the CNS which fades out when axons reach into the neuropil.
source: In contrast, expression of Flp in all sensory neurons using Chat-Gal4 UAS-flp reveals an even Para decoration of axons as they enter the CNS which fades out when axons reach into the neuropil (Figure 2I,I', arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 2I and I' showing Para localization in sensory neurons.

claim: In adult nerves, ParamCherry localization distal to the AIS is found in a clustered arrangement.
source: In adult nerves, ParamCherry localization distal to the AIS is found in a clustered arrangement (Figure 3A–B', arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 3A–B' showing clustered Para localization.

claim: In primary Drosophila neural cell cultures, Para channels are localized in small clusters with a spacing of about 0.6–0.8 µm.
source: When such cultures are stained for Para distribution, we find Para channels localized in small clusters with a spacing of about 0.6–0.8 µm.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from primary neural cell cultures.

claim: Para clusters are about 0.6–0.8 µm apart in adult nerves.
source: Note the clustered appearance of ParamCherry, clusters are about 0.6–0.8 µm apart (arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 3A' showing clustered Para localization with spacing measurements.

claim: Super-resolution imaging of single motor axons decorated with GFP-tagged Para showed an average spacing of 0.620 µm.
source: Further super-resolution imaging of single motor axons decorated with GFP-tagged Para showed an average spacing of 0.620 µm (Figure 3F, F', and G, n=91 clusters on 3 axons, quantification using Fiji).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 3F, F', and G showing super-resolution imaging data with quantification.

claim: Para clusters appear to be organized along lines at the motor axon.
source: Interestingly, Para clusters appear to be organized along lines at the motor axon which was also found when analyzing the distribution of Para at the electron microscopic level (see below).
evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution imaging data and electron microscopy observations.

claim: In multidendritic sensory neurons, low levels of Para protein localize to the cell body and the distal shaft of the axon.
source: For this we expressed flp in multidendritic sensory neurons using the pickpocket Gal4 driver (ppk-Gal4). This allows labeling of the v'ada neurons (Figure 4A). Low levels of Para protein localize to the cell body and the distal shaft of the axon.
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 4A showing Para localization in v'ada neurons.

claim: Along the descending axon of v'ada neurons, Para localization increases only in some distance to the soma.
source: Along the descending axon, Para localization increases only in some distance to the soma (Figure 4A, B, and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 4A, B, and C showing Para localization along the axon.

claim: Para expression in sensory neurons is not as strong as in motor axons.
source: However, para expression in sensory neurons is not as strong as in motor axons which may correspond to the notion that sensory axons are usually smaller axons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that sensory axons are smaller and show lower Para expression.

claim: Within some of the v'ada dendrites, Para accumulates in distinct clusters.
source: Interestingly, however, within some of the v'ada dendrites, Para accumulates in distinct clusters (Figure 4A' and B', arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 4A' and B' showing Para clusters in dendrites.

claim: An AIS is present in Drosophila motor and sensory axons.
source: In conclusion, the above data show the presence of an AIS in Drosophila motor and sensory axons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the localization patterns of Para channels in motor and sensory neurons.

claim: In motor axons, the AIS likely serves as a spike initiation zone.
source: In motor axons, where this domain likely serves as a spike initiation zone (Günay et al., 2015), Para channels are organized in a clustered arrangement.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Günay et al., 2015.

claim: Para channels in motor axons are organized in a clustered arrangement.
source: In motor axons, where this domain likely serves as a spike initiation zone (Günay et al., 2015), Para channels are organized in a clustered arrangement.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing clustered Para localization.

claim: The insertion of an Apex2 encoding exon in the N-terminus of Para affected para function less strongly than the insertion of an mCherry exon.
source: The insertion of an Apex2 encoding exon in the N-terminus of Para affected para function less strongly than the insertion of an mCherry exon and resulted in a very weak hypomorphic para allele (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 1A and B showing the insertion sites and functional assays.

claim: In adult flies, ParaApex2 is expressed in sufficient intensity to be detected along axons using the electron microscope.
source: In adult flies, ParaApex2 is expressed in sufficient intensity to be detected along axons using the electron microscope.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing ParaApex2 localization.

claim: In small diameter peripheral axonal segments, weak ParaApex2 directed DAB precipitates are found.
source: In small diameter peripheral axonal segments, weak ParaApex2 directed DAB precipitates are found (Figure 5A, white arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 5A showing DAB precipitates in small axons.

claim: In large diameter axons next to the CNS/PNS boundary intense DAB precipitates can be detected.
source: In contrast, in large diameter axons next to the CNS/PNS boundary intense DAB precipitates can be detected (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 5B showing intense DAB precipitates in large axons.

claim: The intensity of DAB labeling varied in serial sections, possibly reflecting the clustered localization of Para.
source: When we performed serial sectioning, the intensity of DAB labeling varied (Figure 5B–D), possibly reflecting the clustered localization of Para that we had found using the confocal microscope.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the variation in DAB labeling intensity and is supported by Figures 5B–D.

claim: ParaApex2 clusters are organized in two lines along the ≈2.4 µm axonal circumference.
source: The resulting surface plot shows ParaApex2 localization of a small segment of the axon in a 3D space. This suggests that ParaApex2 clusters are organized in two lines along the ≈2.4 µm axonal circumference (Figure 5F and G), resembling the distribution of ParamCherry clusters along lines as detected using super-resolution light microscopy (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 5F and G showing 3D surface plots of ParaApex2 distribution.

claim: Longitudinal sections of Para-rich axon segments show a spacing of ParaApex2 clusters of 0.706 µm.
source: Here, again a spatial modulation of the Para staining intensity is apparent, with a spacing of 0.706 µm (Figure 5I; see Figure 3G for quantification, n=54 cluster distances on 6 axons), which is similar to what we determined by confocal microscopy.
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 5I and 3G showing quantification of cluster spacing.

claim: Large caliber axons decorated with highest levels of Para protein are embedded in a mesh-like glial organization resembling the lacunar system.
source: Interestingly, the large caliber axons decorated with highest levels of Para protein are embedded in a mesh-like glial organization, that resembles the lacunar system described earlier for the cockroach (Figure 5B–D, Figure 6A, B; Wigglesworth, 1960).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 5B–D and 6A, B showing the lacunar system and a citation to Wigglesworth, 1960.

claim: The Drosophila glial lacunar system is characterized by intensive formation of glial processes around axons which are always larger than 0.5 µm in diameter.
source: The Drosophila glial lacunar system is characterized by intensive formation of glial processes around axons which are always larger than 0.5 µm in diameter (Figure 6A, B, asterisks).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 6A and B showing the lacunar system around large axons.

claim: Glial cell processes in the lacunar system have an average thickness of 35 nm.
source: Glial cell processes have an average thickness of 35 nm (Figure 6A, B, n=189 processes, 4 nerves from 3 animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 6A and B with quantification of glial process thickness.

claim: Most of the lacunar system is generated by tract glial cell processes.
source: To further determine which glial cell forms the lacunar structures, we generated flies harboring a UAS-Myr-Flag-Apex2-NES transgene (Apex2Myr, see Materials and methods) and expressed the myristoylated Apex2 with the different Gal4 drivers mentioned above. These experiments confirmed that most of the lacunar system is indeed generated by tract glial cell processes (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 6A and B showing Apex2 labeling of tract glia.

claim: In large caliber motor axons, most of the Para voltage-gated sodium channels is positioned close to the lacunar system.
source: Thus, in large caliber motor axons, most of the Para voltage-gated sodium channels is positioned close to the lacunar system, which had been previously speculated to serve as an extracellular ion reservoir needed for sustained generation of action potentials (Chandra and Singh, 1983; Leech and Swales, 1987; Maddrell and Treherne, 1967; Treherne and Schofield, 1981; Van Harreveld et al., 1969; Wigglesworth, 1960).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the co-localization of Para channels and the lacunar system, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The lacunar system has been previously speculated to serve as an extracellular ion reservoir needed for sustained generation of action potentials.
source: Thus, in large caliber motor axons, most of the Para voltage-gated sodium channels is positioned close to the lacunar system, which had been previously speculated to serve as an extracellular ion reservoir needed for sustained generation of action potentials (Chandra and Singh, 1983; Leech and Swales, 1987; Maddrell and Treherne, 1967; Treherne and Schofield, 1981; Van Harreveld et al., 1969; Wigglesworth, 1960).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chandra and Singh, 1983; Leech and Swales, 1987; Maddrell and Treherne, 1967; Treherne and Schofield, 1981; Van Harreveld et al., 1969; Wigglesworth, 1960.

claim: In vertebrates, clustering of voltage-gated ion channels occurs on the edges of myelinated axonal segments (internodes).
source: In vertebrates, clustering of voltage-gated ion channels occurs on the edges of myelinated axonal segments (internodes) (Arancibia-Cárcamo et al., 2017; Castelfranco and Hartline, 2015; Cohen et al., 2020; Dutta et al., 2018; Eshed-Eisenbach and Peles, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Arancibia-Cárcamo et al., 2017; Castelfranco and Hartline, 2015; Cohen et al., 2020; Dutta et al., 2018; Eshed-Eisenbach and Peles, 2021.

claim: In vertebrates, myelin participates in positioning of voltage-gated ion channels.
source: Here, myelin not only participates in positioning of voltage-gated ion channels but also increases electric insulation and thus contributes to a faster conductance velocity.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about vertebrate myelin function.

claim: In vertebrates, myelin increases electric insulation and contributes to a faster conductance velocity.
source: Here, myelin not only participates in positioning of voltage-gated ion channels but also increases electric insulation and thus contributes to a faster conductance velocity.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about vertebrate myelin function.

claim: Most of the 760 axons within an adult leg run in a single large nerve that exit the CNS at well-defined positions.
source: Most of the 760 axons within an adult leg run in a single large nerve that exit the CNS at well-defined positions (Figure 7A-C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 7A-C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A showing the leg nerve anatomy.

claim: Unlike the organization in larval nerves, axons running in the leg nerves are found in distinct zones depending on their diameter.
source: Unlike the organization in larval nerves, axons running in the leg nerves are found in distinct zones depending on their diameter (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 7B and C showing axon organization in leg nerves.

claim: At the position of the femur, large axons are always covered by a single glial sheet.
source: At the position of the femur, large axons are always covered by a single glial sheet.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy observations.

claim: Small diameter axons are generally not individually wrapped but rather engulfed as a fascicle.
source: Small diameter axons are generally not individually wrapped but rather engulfed as a fascicle (Figure 7B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 7B and D showing axon wrapping patterns.

claim: At the coxa, close to the CNS, large diameter axons are occasionally flanked by several glial membrane sheets.
source: At the coxa, close to the CNS, we noted that large diameter axons were occasionally flanked by several glial membrane sheets (Figure 7E, asterisk).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 7E showing multiple glial wraps around axons.

claim: Up to 15 flat glial membrane sheets with a thickness of about 28 nm are found along larger axons.
source: Up to 15 flat glial membrane sheets with a thickness of about 28 nm are found along larger axons (Figure 7E,F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 7E, F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B showing myelin-like structures with quantification.

claim: An increase in the number of myelin-like structures is noted at the distal end of the lacunae.
source: Here, we noted an increase in the number of myelin-like structures at the distal end of the lacunae (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B, Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 2B and Figure 7—figure supplement 3 showing quantification of myelin-like structures.

claim: No myelin-like structures were found at proximal positions close to the neuropil.
source: No myelin-like structures were found at proximal positions close to the neuropil.
evidence: The claim is supported by serial section analysis.

claim: Upon expression of Apex2Myr in CNS-derived tract glia, DAB positive myelin stacks can be detected.
source: Upon expression of Apex2Myr in CNS-derived tract glia 75H03-Gal4 DAB positive myelin stacks can be detected (Figure 7G (black arrowhead), Figure 7I, Figure 7—figure supplement 3, Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 7G, 7I, Figure 7—figure supplement 3, and Figure 7—figure supplement 5 showing DAB-labeled myelin stacks.

claim: Peripheral wrapping glial cells can form myelin-like structures in the leg nerve.
source: The finding that 75H03-Gal4 directed Apex2 labeling can be found next to unlabeled glial sheets (Figure 7G, white arrowhead) suggests that peripheral wrapping glial cells can also form myelin-like structures in the leg nerve.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the presence of unlabeled glial sheets next to labeled ones, supported by Figure 7G.

claim: Drosophila myelin-like membrane stacks are generated by extensive membrane folding.
source: Drosophila myelin-like membrane stacks are generated by extensive membrane folding providing the disadvantage that axons are not entirely insulated (Figure 7I, Figure 7—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 7I and Figure 7—figure supplements 4 and 5 showing membrane folding patterns.

claim: Axons are not entirely insulated by Drosophila myelin-like structures.
source: Drosophila myelin-like membrane stacks are generated by extensive membrane folding providing the disadvantage that axons are not entirely insulated (Figure 7I, Figure 7—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the membrane folding pattern and is supported by Figure 7I and Figure 7—figure supplements 4 and 5.

claim: Axons encircled by multiple glial wraps are occasionally found.
source: However, we occasionally do find axons encircled by multiple glial wraps (Figure 7H, Figure 7—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 7H and Figure 7—figure supplements 4 and 5 showing axons with multiple wraps.

claim: In some areas, almost compacted glial membrane sheets are noted.
source: Interestingly, in some areas we noted almost compacted glial membrane sheets (Figure 7F,I, inlay boxed areas).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 7F and I showing compacted membrane sheets.

claim: In compacted areas, the interperiodic distance of the different glial layers is about 30 nm.
source: In the compacted areas (Figure 7I–K), the interperiodic distance of the different glial layers is about 30 nm, which is considerably more than the interperiodic distance of 13 nm found in mouse peripheral myelin (Fledrich et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figures 7I–K showing compacted areas with measurements and a citation to Fledrich et al., 2018.

claim: The interperiodic distance of 13 nm is found in mouse peripheral myelin.
source: In the compacted areas (Figure 7I–K), the interperiodic distance of the different glial layers is about 30 nm, which is considerably more than the interperiodic distance of 13 nm found in mouse peripheral myelin (Fledrich et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fledrich et al., 2018.

claim: The unique compact appearance of vertebrate myelin is mediated by the myelin basic protein (MBP).
source: The unique compact appearance of vertebrate myelin is mediated by the myelin basic protein (MBP) (Nave and Werner, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nave and Werner, 2021.

claim: Fly myelin-like structures only show an irregular compaction of the extracellular space.
source: In contrast to vertebrate myelin where extra- and intercellular space is removed, fly myelin-like structures only show an irregular compaction of the extracellular space.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison with vertebrate myelin and electron microscopy observations.

claim: A fully compact myelin state would require MBP-like proteins which have not been identified in the fly genome.
source: A fully compact myelin state would require MBP-like proteins which have not been identified in the fly genome.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the fly genome and the absence of MBP-like proteins.

claim: Ablation of central or peripheral wrapping glial cells does not affect the distribution of the voltage-gated potassium channel Shal.
source: Ablation of central or peripheral wrapping glial cells does not affect the distribution of the voltage-gated potassium channel Shal (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 1 showing Shal localization in glia-ablated larvae.

claim: Removal of the CNS-specific ensheathing glia does not affect Para localization in the larval nervous system.
source: Likewise, removal of the CNS-specific ensheathing glia does not affect Para localization in the larval nervous system (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–E showing Para localization after ensheathing glia ablation.

claim: Upon ablation of the peripheral wrapping glia, a marked change in Para protein localization becomes obvious.
source: In contrast, upon ablation of the peripheral wrapping glia a marked change in Para protein localization becomes obvious (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–B').
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–B' showing Para localization after wrapping glia ablation.

claim: In wild type control larvae, 2.5 times more Para protein is found at the CNS/PNS transition zone compared to nerve segments on the muscle field.
source: Whereas in wild type control larvae, 2.5 times more Para protein is found at the CNS/PNS transition zone compared to nerve segments on the muscle field, an almost even distribution is noted in glia ablated larvae (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 8C showing quantification of Para fluorescence intensity.

claim: An almost even distribution of Para is noted in glia ablated larvae.
source: Whereas in wild type control larvae, 2.5 times more Para protein is found at the CNS/PNS transition zone compared to nerve segments on the muscle field, an almost even distribution is noted in glia ablated larvae (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 8C showing quantification of Para fluorescence intensity.

claim: A twofold increase of para mRNA levels is noted in wrapping glia ablated larvae.
source: In addition to the redistribution of Para protein along the axon, we also noted a twofold increase of para mRNA levels in further qRT-PCR experiments (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 8D showing qRT-PCR data.

claim: In Drosophila, para mRNA expression depends on the presence of peripheral wrapping glia.
source: Interestingly, in Drosophila para mRNA expression as well as Para protein localization depend on the presence of peripheral wrapping glia.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing increased para mRNA in glia-ablated larvae.

claim: In Drosophila, Para protein localization depends on the presence of peripheral wrapping glia.
source: Interestingly, in Drosophila para mRNA expression as well as Para protein localization depend on the presence of peripheral wrapping glia.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing altered Para localization in glia-ablated larvae.

claim: In glia ablated nerves, Para expression is increased and decorates the entire axonal membrane.
source: In glia ablated nerves, Para expression is increased and decorates the entire axonal membrane.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and qRT-PCR data.

claim: The loss of a clustered distribution of Para may contribute to the pronounced reduction in axonal conductance velocity noted in glia ablated animals.
source: This loss of a clustered distribution may contribute to the pronounced reduction in axonal conductance velocity noted earlier in such glia ablated animals (Kottmeier et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the altered Para distribution and is supported by a citation to Kottmeier et al., 2020.

claim: Alterations in glial differentiation caused by manipulation of FGF-receptor signaling specifically in peripheral wrapping glia does not cause a change in Para expression or localization.
source: Since alterations in glial differentiation caused by manipulation of FGF-receptor signaling specifically in peripheral wrapping glia does not cause a change in Para expression or localization (Figure 8—figure supplement 2F–H), proteins secreted by wrapping glia might be needed for the correct positioning of voltage-gated ion channels (Yuan and Ganetzky, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 2F–H showing Para localization after FGF-receptor manipulation.

claim: Proteins secreted by wrapping glia might be needed for the correct positioning of voltage-gated ion channels.
source: Since alterations in glial differentiation caused by manipulation of FGF-receptor signaling specifically in peripheral wrapping glia does not cause a change in Para expression or localization (Figure 8—figure supplement 2F–H), proteins secreted by wrapping glia might be needed for the correct positioning of voltage-gated ion channels (Yuan and Ganetzky, 1999).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and inference, supported by a citation to Yuan and Ganetzky, 1999.

claim: In the adult nervous system, the AIS-like domain is embedded in glial lacunar regions formed by wrapping glial cell processes.
source: In the adult nervous system, the AIS-like domain is embedded in glial lacunar regions formed by wrapping glial cell processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy and immunohistochemistry data.

claim: The increased expression of Para within the AIS-like segments of adult brains is expected to generate strong ephaptic coupling forces.
source: The increased expression of Para within the AIS-like segments of adult brains is expected to generate strong ephaptic coupling forces (Rey et al., 2022; Rey et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and is supported by citations to Rey et al., 2022 and Rey et al., 2021.

claim: Ephaptic coupling is caused by ion flux through open channels which generate an electric field that is able to influence the gating of ion channels in closely neighboring axons.
source: These are caused by ion flux through open channels which generate an electric field that is able to influence the gating of ion channels in closely neighboring axons (Arvanitaki, 1942; Krnjevic, 1986; Rasminsky, 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Arvanitaki, 1942; Krnjevic, 1986; Rasminsky, 1980.

claim: Ephaptic coupling helps to synchronize firing axons.
source: Ephaptic coupling helps to synchronize firing axons (Anastassiou and Koch, 2015; Anastassiou et al., 2011; Han et al., 2018; Shneider and Pekker, 2015), but is also detrimental to the precision of neuronal signaling in closely apposed axons (Arvanitaki, 1942; Kottmeier et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Anastassiou and Koch, 2015; Anastassiou et al., 2011; Han et al., 2018; Shneider and Pekker, 2015.

claim: Ephaptic coupling is detrimental to the precision of neuronal signaling in closely apposed axons.
source: Ephaptic coupling helps to synchronize firing axons (Anastassiou and Koch, 2015; Anastassiou et al., 2011; Han et al., 2018; Shneider and Pekker, 2015), but is also detrimental to the precision of neuronal signaling in closely apposed axons (Arvanitaki, 1942; Kottmeier et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Arvanitaki, 1942 and Kottmeier et al., 2020.

claim: Ephaptic coupling is counteracted by the glial lacunar system.
source: Ephaptic coupling is counteracted by the glial lacunar system, that spatially separates axons and adds more levels of wrapping.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the structure and function of the lacunar system.

claim: The lacunar system spatially separates axons and adds more levels of wrapping.
source: Ephaptic coupling is counteracted by the glial lacunar system, that spatially separates axons and adds more levels of wrapping.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing the structure of the lacunar system.

claim: The lacunar system provides a large extracellular ion reservoir.
source: Furthermore, it was postulated that the lacunar system provides a large extracellular ion reservoir (Wigglesworth, 1960).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wigglesworth, 1960.
